questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: What Makes a State a State
questions.learningObjective: state what is being compared when two states are called different
questions.stem: Two conditions are described as different states of consciousness. What has to be true for that description to mean anything?

options.text: That both the person's own report and their measured behaviour differ from the pattern seen in the other condition
That the person has been asked which state they are in and has named it correctly
options.misconception: makes a state a matter of correct self-classification

options.text: That the person is unconscious, since a conscious person could not reliably say which state they are in
options.misconception: requires unconsciousness before a state can be identified

options.text: That the two conditions were measured with different instruments, since one instrument cannot show a change
options.misconception: makes a change of state require a change of apparatus

questions.explanation: A state is a pattern, and the word only earns its keep when the pattern can be specified rather than named. The two things that can be specified are what the person says and what the person's behaviour and physiological record do, and neither on its own is sufficient. A report is a report and can be produced by expectation, by a suggestion and by a wish to please the person asking, which is why a first-person classification is not evidence of a state. Behaviour and a physiological record are independent of how willing a person is to describe anything, and when the two kinds of evidence move together a state has been identified rather than asserted. The other readings each substitute a single unreliable source for the pair. The requirement that a person be unconscious is the opposite of what is wanted, since many states of interest are defined by a report of an unusual experience. And an instrument that failed to show a change last time is a fact about the instrument, which is a reason to change instruments rather than a reason to deny the state.
questions.hint: Ask what two independent sources of evidence have to agree on before a difference counts as a state.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: Ordering a Continuum From No Response to Full Alertness
questions.learningObjective: order states of arousal from unresponsive wakefulness to alert waking
questions.stem: Put these five conditions in order, from the one with the least evidence of awareness to the one with the most.

options.text: A vegetative state, in which eyes open and track but there is no reliable evidence of awareness
A confused waking state, in which a person is awake but does not make sense of where they are
Drowsiness, in which a person can be roused by a sound and answers slowly
Alert wakefulness, in which a person sustains attention and responds to what is said to them
Coma, in which a person cannot be roused by a sound or a touch and shows no purposeful response

questions.explanation: The ordering follows the evidence of awareness, and the two middle positions are where most of the difficulty lies. Coma comes first because the defining feature is absent responsiveness to stimulation that ought to rouse anyone, with no sign that awareness is present underneath. The vegetative state comes next and is the item that makes the scale instructive: eyes open and track a person across a room, which looks like waking and is not, since the wakefulness is there and the awareness is not reliably there, and repeated assessment is what establishes the absence rather than any single observation. Confused waking sits above it because some genuine comprehension is present even though it is disorganised, and drowsiness sits above that because the person can be brought to a conversation and hold it briefly. Alert wakefulness is the top of this scale and is a reference point rather than a peak, since the scale is a continuum and a person in a crowd or in pain can be awake without being alert. The order that puts waking above the vegetative state because of the eye movements mistakes an observable behaviour for the awareness it usually accompanies.
questions.hint: Order by how much evidence of awareness is present, not by how much of the person can be seen moving.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: Conditions Distinguished by Their Evidence of Awareness
questions.learningObjective: distinguish clinical conditions by what they show and what they rule out
questions.stem: Four conditions are described. Which pair of statements about them is correct? Select both.

options.text: A vegetative state shows wakefulness without reliable evidence of awareness, and that combination is what makes it hard to diagnose
Brain death is a legal finding of irreversible loss of function, and it is the one condition on this list from which no recovery is possible
Brain death is diagnosed by looking at the movements of the eyes, and the eye movements are the criterion involved
options.misconception: describes the eye movements of a waking person as the criterion for brain death

options.text: Locked-in syndrome leaves a person's intelligence unaffected, so the loss is of movement and speech alone
options.misconception: claims the person's thinking is untouched, ignoring what the damage can reach

questions.explanation: The four conditions are separated by two questions: is there any awareness, and is there any prospect of recovery. A vegetative state answers the first question in the negative while the person appears awake, since eyes open and track, which is exactly the combination that makes it difficult to diagnose on a single examination, so repeated assessment over time is part of the practice and the diagnosis is revised when the evidence changes. Brain death answers the second question: it is a determination of irreversible loss of all brain function, made on a defined protocol and, in the jurisdictions that use it, a legal death. That is a stronger claim than coma or a vegetative state, both of which can improve. The third statement inverts things, since the eye movements that characterize a waking person are exactly what brain death excludes, and it is the absence of responses to a range of tests that carries the diagnosis. The fourth statement is close to the description of locked-in syndrome and wrong in its first clause: a person who is locked in is awake, aware and often cognitively intact, while the damage has reached the pathways controlling movement, so the description belongs to a different condition and the intelligence claim overreaches.
questions.hint: Ask two questions of each condition: is awareness present, and can the condition improve?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: What a Sleep Stage Is Decided From
questions.learningObjective: state what the three channels of a sleep record contribute to staging
questions.stem: A sleep record is made with three kinds of measurement taken together: a tracing of the electrical activity of the brain, another of the movement of the eyes, and a third of the tension in the neck muscles. Why are all three needed?

options.text: The eye channel replaces the brain channel during rapid eye movement sleep, when the two disagree
options.misconception: lets one channel overrule the other instead of contributing its own information

options.text: Each separates a state the others cannot, since brain activity alone cannot tell movement from stillness at the eyes or a still body from a tense one
Each is required by the rules of the laboratory, so a two-channel record cannot be scored at all
options.misconception: makes the third channel a rule of scoring rather than a source of information

options.text: They are averaged into a single index, since a stage is best described by one combined number
options.misconception: combines the channels into one figure rather than reading them together

questions.explanation: A stage is defined by a pattern across the three channels, and the reason each one is there is that the stages it distinguishes are identical in some channels and different only in another. Brain activity alone cannot tell rapid eye movement sleep from wakefulness, since the two look broadly similar in a brain tracing, and the eye channel is what separates them. Brain activity alone also cannot distinguish the two lighter stages from each other or from drowsiness in the way a well-scored record requires, and the muscle channel contributes there as well, since muscle tension falls as sleep deepens and is at its lowest during rapid eye movement sleep. The muscle channel is also what makes the paralysis of that stage visible as a record rather than an inference, since a low tension channel during vigorous eye movements is the signature of the two happening together. The rule-based reading misdescribes a practice whose content is discriminating information, and averaging the channels into a number would throw away exactly the joint pattern the scoring depends on.
questions.hint: Ask which two states look the same in the brain tracing, and what the other channels show about them.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: Naming an Oscillation From Its Frequency
questions.learningObjective: place a frequency within the conventional bands of the brain record

stimulus.body: Conventional bands of the brain electrical record: delta 0.5 to 4 Hz, theta 4 to 8 Hz, alpha 8 to 13 Hz, beta 13 to 30 Hz, gamma 30 to 100 Hz. Six oscillations are recorded with the following frequencies: 2 Hz, 4 Hz, 9 Hz, 13 Hz, 20 Hz and 45 Hz. Which band contains each one?
stimulus.license: written for this question; no third-party material

questions.stem: A brain record shows six oscillations at 2, 4, 9, 13, 20 and 45 Hz. Using the conventional bands, which set of assignments is right?

options.text: 2 in delta, 4 in delta, 9 in alpha, 13 in alpha, 20 in beta and 45 in beta
options.misconception: assigns each value to the band below the one whose lower boundary it reaches

options.text: 2 in gamma, 4 in beta, 9 in alpha, 13 in theta, 20 in delta and 45 in delta
options.misconception: reverses the order of the bands so that the fastest read as the slowest

options.text: 2 in delta, 4 in theta, 9 in alpha, 13 in beta, 20 in beta and 45 in gamma
2 in theta, 4 in alpha, 9 in beta, 13 in gamma, 20 in gamma and 45 in gamma
options.misconception: shifts every assignment up one band, as if the lower boundary of each band were exclusive

questions.explanation: The bands are contiguous, which is worth checking before using them: delta ends at 4 and theta begins at 4, theta ends at 8 and alpha begins at 8, alpha ends at 13 and beta begins at 13, and beta ends at 30 and gamma begins at 30, so no frequency is left out and no frequency is claimed twice. An oscillation at 2 sits inside delta, since 2 is above 0.5 and below 4. An oscillation at 4 sits at the delta and theta boundary and belongs to theta, because a band owns its lower boundary, and that convention is what keeps the five bands a partition rather than an overlapping set. The same rule puts 9 in alpha, 13 in beta and 20 in beta, while 45 is above 30 and so is gamma. The second option applies the rule backwards, treating a lower boundary as belonging to the band below, which is a different convention and would leave 4, 9 and 13 unassigned. The remaining two options misplace the bands wholesale, one by shifting up and one by reversing the order.
questions.hint: Check that the bands join end to end, then ask which band owns each shared boundary.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: Reading a Night as a Graph
questions.learningObjective: state what a hypnogram shows and what it does not
questions.stem: A night of sleep is drawn as a stair of labelled horizontal bands, one per stage, plotted against time. What does that drawing let a reader see that a single night's total would hide?

options.text: How deeply the person slept in general, since one night stands for a person's usual pattern
options.misconception: treats a single night as a representative record of a person's habit

options.text: What the person was dreaming, since the graph's segments are coded for dream content
options.misconception: reads the stage bands as codes for the content of a dream

options.text: Whether the record is genuine, since a fabricated record would have an irregular shape
options.misconception: treats the shape of the trace as a test of whether the record is real

options.text: The order in which the stages were entered and how long each was held, which a total cannot show

questions.explanation: The drawing exists because a night is a sequence and a total is a single number, so the two answer different questions and only one of them is about the sequence. With the stages plotted against time a reader sees how many times the person passed through deep sleep, where in the night the long stretches of light sleep sat, how the stages were distributed across the first and second halves, and how long any arousal lasted. That is information a total destroys, and it is why the figure is drawn rather than tabulated. The limits are worth naming in the same breath. A hypnogram is one night, and a single night varies considerably from person to person and from occasion to occasion, so a pattern in one record is a description of that night rather than a profile of the sleeper. It carries nothing about what was dreamed; the stages are scored from the record, not from any content. And the shape is not a signature, since a fabricated record can have a plausible shape and a genuine one can look irregular.
questions.hint: Ask what a sequence shows that a sum cannot, and then what a single night's record generalises to.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: The Repeating Unit of a Night
questions.learningObjective: describe the structure of a single sleep cycle
questions.stem: A night's sleep is not a single descent and a single climb. What is the repeating unit that gives it its structure?

options.text: A single continuous descent into deep sleep that is held until morning, with no return to lighter stages
options.misconception: describes an unbroken descent with no cycling back toward light sleep

options.text: An alternation between rapid eye movement sleep and wakefulness, with the non-rapid stages occurring only at the start
options.misconception: moves the non-rapid stages to the beginning and leaves the rest of the night in two states

options.text: A single descent and a single climb, so a night's sleep is one cycle repeated at a different depth each time
options.misconception: makes the whole night a single cycle that changes depth

options.text: A descent from light sleep through deeper stages, then a period of rapid eye movement sleep, after which the cycle starts again

questions.explanation: The night is built from a repeating cycle of roughly an hour and a half, and the shape of that cycle is what the word structure means here. Within a cycle sleep descends from light sleep through the deeper stages, then becomes rapid eye movement sleep, in which the brain is active, the eyes move, muscle tone is at its lowest and dreams are reported most often, and the cycle then begins again from the light stages. A typical night contains about four to five of these cycles, which is what makes the sleep a series rather than a single act of losing consciousness. The other readings each flatten the sequence. Holding deep sleep until morning describes a chart that does not exist in anyone's record, since deep sleep is a minority of the night. Putting the non-rapid stages only at the start describes a night that ends in rapid eye movement sleep continuously, and while rapid eye movement sleep does lengthen towards morning the other stages are present throughout. The single-cycle reading gets the right ingredients and puts them in the wrong arrangement, since a cycle is by construction something that repeats.
questions.hint: Ask what the record does after a period of rapid eye movement sleep ends.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: A Night Broken Into Minutes by Stage
questions.learningObjective: read stage totals and shares off a night's record

stimulus.body: One night of recording from a volunteer in a sleep laboratory, in 30-second epochs. Awake: 20 epochs. Stage 1: 20 epochs. Stage 2: 240 epochs. Stage 3: 45 epochs. Rapid eye movement sleep: 95 epochs. Total: 420 epochs, which is 420 minutes.
stimulus.license: written for this question; no third-party material

questions.stem: One night of laboratory recording gives 20 minutes awake, 20 in stage 1, 240 in stage 2, 45 in stage 3 and 95 in rapid eye movement sleep. What follows from those figures?

options.text: The recording covers 420 minutes, and stage 2 is more than half of it at 57 percent
The recording covers 440 minutes, since the five stage figures are 20, 20, 240, 45 and 95
options.misconception: misadds the five stage figures

options.text: The recording covers 420 minutes, and the deep stage is the largest share at 45 percent
options.misconception: reads the 45 minutes of stage 3 as 45 percent of the night

options.text: The recording covers 400 minutes, since the 20 minutes awake fall outside the night and are excluded
options.misconception: excludes the awake epochs from the recording altogether

questions.explanation: The figures add to 420 minutes, which is seven hours, and the shares follow from dividing each figure by that total. Stage 2 at 240 minutes is 240 over 420, which is 57 percent, so light sleep is more than half of a typical recording, and that is the single most underappreciated fact about the architecture. The deep stage at 45 minutes is about 11 percent, rapid eye movement sleep at 95 minutes is about 23 percent, and awake at 20 minutes is about 5 percent, the last three being rounded shares of the same 420-minute total. The remaining distractor takes the 45 minutes of stage 3 and reads the digits as a percentage, which is a quick way to be wrong by a factor of four; the deep stage is the smallest of the three sleep stages, not the largest. The other two make errors in the bookkeeping, one by adding the figures incorrectly and one by deleting the awake epochs from the recording when the question asks what the recording contains. It is worth holding on to the share figure rather than the minutes, since the minutes depend on how long the person happened to lie there.
questions.hint: Add the five figures first, then divide each by the total rather than reading a percentage off a number.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: What the Second Stage of Sleep Contains
questions.learningObjective: identify the features of stage 2 and what they are proposed to do
questions.stem: Stage 2 occupies more of a night than any other sleep stage. Which features identify it, and what have they been proposed to support?

options.text: A mixture of low-amplitude activity and slow waves with no distinctive events, which makes it unscoreable
options.misconception: denies the stage any scorable signature of its own

options.text: Bursts of faster activity lasting about a second and a large slow wave, which have been proposed as helping new learning
Very slow waves at under four hertz and a complete loss of muscle tone, which mark the deepest stage
options.misconception: assigns the features of the deep stage to the second stage

options.text: Fast low-amplitude activity with rapid eye movements and no slow waves, which identifies the dreaming stage
options.misconception: moves the features of rapid eye movement sleep into the second stage

questions.explanation: Stage 2 has a signature that the scoring rules rely on, and the signature is a pair of events. The first is a burst of faster activity lasting about a second, and the second is a large slow wave, and a stage is scored as 2 rather than 1 by the presence of at least one of them, which is why the stage is not simply a matter of how slow the record looks. The proposal about what they do is that these events are associated with the processing of new material, and the association is supported in the sense that they occur during sleep and that their timing falls in the part of the night when learning in the preceding day is thought to be consolidated, with the sharpest relationship found for material that had been learned rather than merely encountered. What should be said about the claim is where its status lies: the correlation is well documented and the idea of a role in learning is a live account of it, but demonstrating that the bursts are necessary for learning would require interrupting them, and that experiment has produced mixed results. The other options each describe a different stage, or deny the stage a signature it plainly has.
questions.hint: Ask which two events the scoring rules actually look for, and where in the night they occur.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: An Account of Sleep Spindles That Is Still Open
questions.learningObjective: state the proposal linking sleep spindles to learning and what would test it
questions.stem: Bursts of faster brain activity during stage 2 have been linked to the learning that happened earlier in the day. How should the strength of that link be described?

options.text: As a settled question, since sleep spindles appear in every normal sleeper and so cannot be a coincidence
options.misconception: treats universality as evidence of a function

options.text: As refuted, since suppression of the bursts leaves learning intact in the experiments that have been run
options.misconception: turns mixed experimental results into a refutation

options.text: As a well-documented association, with the causal role still to be shown by changing the bursts and seeing whether learning survives
As an established fact, since the bursts occur in the same sleep stage in which consolidation is thought to happen
options.misconception: converts a temporal coincidence into a demonstrated cause

questions.explanation: The evidence for the link is of two kinds, and it helps to keep them apart. The correlational evidence is consistent and repeated: the bursts occur during stage 2, they are more numerous and more tightly coupled to particular brain oscillations after a day in which material was learned than after a day without it, and the size of that increase tracks the amount that was learned. That is a real relationship and it is not a coincidence in any useful sense. The causal claim is a different matter, because the natural test is to interfere with the bursts during sleep and see whether retention falls, and the experiments doing that have produced inconsistent results, complicated by the fact that suppressing an oscillation may change the rest of the night's architecture. The honest summary is that the association is documented and the mechanism is proposed. The remaining readings each jump to a conclusion: coincidence in time is not cause, universality across sleepers says nothing about function, and mixed results are not a refutation, and naming the experiment that would decide it is what distinguishes an open question from a closed one.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of evidence exists, and what experiment would move the claim from association to cause.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: What Changes in the Dreaming Stage
questions.learningObjective: state the physiological features of rapid eye movement sleep
questions.stem: Which set of findings characterises the stage in which most dream reports are collected?

options.text: An active brain, no eye movement and high muscle tone, which is the picture of a person sitting still
options.misconception: pairs brain activity with wakefulness-like muscle tone and no eye movement

options.text: A quiet brain, bursts of eye movement and no muscle tone at all, which is what paralysis without dreams would look like
options.misconception: mixes eye movements with a silent brain and complete paralysis

options.text: An active brain, bursts of eye movement, and muscle tone at its lowest, which is also the stage of greatest atonia
A quiet brain, no eye movement and steady muscle tone, which is what the sleeping body looks like from outside
options.misconception: describes the outward appearance and misses the internal activity

questions.explanation: The stage looks like wakefulness from the inside and like paralysis from the outside, and both halves of that description are established findings. Inside, the brain is active in a pattern resembling waking activity, the eyes move in bursts that are related to what the dreamer reports, and the person reports dreams far more often here than in any other stage. Outside, the large muscles are essentially silent, so a person in this stage cannot move their limbs, and the combination of an active brain and a paralysed body is unusual. The second option describes what a sleeping person looks like to an observer and is wrong about the brain and about the eyes. The third pairs the internal activity with the muscle tone of wakefulness, which is the opposite of what happens. The fourth is internally inconsistent, since the eye movements belong with the active brain, and total paralysis with a quiet brain describes neither this stage nor any other. The eye movements matter beyond the description, since their relationship to the dream content is one of the recurring findings about this stage.
questions.hint: Ask what the inside of the body is doing and what the outside of the body is doing at the same time.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: Why Dream Reports From One Stage Are Longer
questions.learningObjective: state the evidence on stage differences in dream recall and the qualifications
questions.stem: Reports collected on waking from a period with rapid eye movement sleep tend to be longer than reports from a period of deep sleep. What accounts for the difference, and what should be said about it?

options.text: A difference in how long each stage lasts, so the stage that lasts longer has more to report
options.misconception: explains the difference by stage duration rather than by recall

options.text: A difference in dreaming itself, since little or nothing is dreamed during deep sleep at all
options.misconception: converts a difference in report length into a claim that no dreaming occurs

options.text: A difference in the reporting itself, since people describe the stage with the eye movements more elaborately
options.misconception: makes the stage effect an artefact of how people talk about the two stages

options.text: A difference in how much can be recalled from each stage, with the recall finding well established and the reason for it still open

questions.explanation: The finding is one of the more reliable in the area and it has two quite separate parts. The descriptive part is well established: awakenings from rapid eye movement sleep produce longer and more narrative reports, and awakenings from the deep stage produce shorter ones and, when they produce anything, more thought-like material, though that last contrast has been harder to replicate than the length difference. The explanatory part is open. Candidates include the involvement of brain systems that differ between the two stages, a difference in how the waking brain is positioned to receive a report, and the fact that a shorter report may reflect a brief episode rather than a poor memory of it. What should be resisted is the step from longer reports to more dreaming, since length is a property of a report and the two are not the same quantity. The two explanations in the distractors are each a specific mistake: duration is a property of the night's plan and cannot explain a difference in what a report contains, and reporting elaborately because one stage is distinctive is a possibility that has been tested by asking people about stages they were not in, with mixed findings.
questions.hint: Separate the descriptive finding from the explanation, and ask what a longer report does and does not show about the experience.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: Whether a Dream Continues the Day
questions.learningObjective: state the debate about continuity between waking experience and dream content
questions.stem: One account says dream content continues the concerns of the waking day, and another says dreams are built from older material and a physiological process of their own. How should the evidence be characterised?

options.text: Daytime concerns do appear in a minority of reports, and the size of that overlap is hard to estimate because of how reports are collected
Daytime concerns appear in most reports, so the continuity account is established and the alternative has been refuted
options.misconception: inflates a minority finding into a refutation of the alternative

options.text: Daytime concerns appear in no reports at all, which is what the physiological account predicts
options.misconception: turns the physiological account into a prediction of total absence

options.text: The two accounts cannot be compared, since dreams are private and no two people report the same one
options.misconception: denies that reports can be compared at all

questions.explanation: This is a live dispute, and the useful thing to know is the shape of the evidence rather than a verdict. There is a real finding in favour of continuity: when people are asked about their dreams after a day in which a particular concern dominated, references to that concern appear in a minority of reports and at a rate well above what an unrelated day would produce, and a small number of controlled studies have found measurable effects of the day's activities on what is reported. The problem is quantification. A study can only detect continuity in the reports it happens to collect, whether because it asked about the day, because it used dream content coding blind to the day's content, or because it woke people often enough to catch short dreams, and the measured overlap changes a great deal with those choices. A physiological account can accommodate some continuity without being refuted by it. The stronger readings all overshoot: a minority does not establish the claim, no reports at all is not what the physiological account predicts, and the fact that dreams are private has never prevented content from being collected and compared across many reports.
questions.hint: Ask how a study could detect continuity, and what would change if the collection method changed.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: Why So Few Dreams Are Remembered in the Morning
questions.learningObjective: explain the methodological reasons dream recall is low
questions.stem: People typically report one or two dreams a week, while laboratory studies that wake people repeatedly find that most awakenings are followed by some dream experience. What accounts for the gap?

options.text: A difference in dream length, since laboratory awakenings catch only dreams that last a full minute
options.misconception: invents a minimum dream length that accounts for the difference

options.text: The waking gap between an experience and a report, during which the content is largely lost, so frequency and recall are different quantities
A difference in the people who volunteer for sleep laboratories, who dream more often than everyone else
options.misconception: explains the gap by a difference in who volunteers

options.text: A difference in how the two studies ask about dreams, since laboratory participants are told what counts as one
options.misconception: makes the whole gap a matter of how the question was worded

questions.explanation: The two figures measure different things, and the difference between them is mostly a property of the measurement rather than of the sleeper. In the laboratory, a report is collected within seconds of an experience, so almost everything that was there can be said; in everyday life there is an interval between waking and telling, and dream material is fragile, so what survives is a fragment or an impression. The reports are also selective, since a fragment that is vivid is reported and a flat one is not, which biases the everyday tally towards memorable content. None of this means that the laboratory figure is the true frequency of dreaming, because the awakenings themselves interrupt the sleep and the brief experiences caught at a random awakening are not necessarily a sample of all experiences. The point is the one about units: a count of remembered dreams is not a count of dreams, and a study that reports one as though it were the other has made a definitional error. The alternatives each invent a difference between the settings that is not needed to explain the gap and is not supported.
questions.hint: Ask how long after the experience each study collects the report.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: How a Report of Dreaming While Awake Is Checked
questions.learningObjective: state the evidence for lucid dreaming and the limits of that evidence
questions.stem: People claim to know that they are dreaming while the dream continues. What is the strongest kind of evidence available for that, and what does it not settle?

options.text: The length of the lucid periods, since a longer period indicates better control and rules out error
options.misconception: takes the length of a period as evidence of accuracy

options.text: The pattern of eye movements reported during the dream, which can be checked against what the report says was being looked at
The person's own certainty, since a dreamer who knows they are dreaming cannot be mistaken about it
options.misconception: accepts the dreamer's certainty as the strongest evidence

options.text: A waking report of having been lucid, since a lucid dream is by definition one the dreamer remembered
options.misconception: treats remembering the dream as evidence of knowing during it

questions.explanation: The problem with self-knowledge in a dream is that there is no external check available, so the evidence has to come from a channel the dreamer does not control, and eye movements are the one that has been used. The reasoning is that in this stage the eyes move in a pattern that is related to what is being looked at in the dream, so a person reporting a lucid dream in which they read a particular pair of digits produces a distinctive pattern of gaze movements, and a laboratory can ask for the digits afterwards and check whether the pattern matches. Where this has been done it has supported the claim, and it is a considerably better design than asking the dreamer how sure they are. What it does not settle is the stronger claim, which is that the dreamer exerts control over what happens next. Reports of control are difficult to verify, since whatever the dreamer decides to do is also what they will describe, and the literature on that is genuinely disputed. The last option is a non sequitur, since the length of a period says nothing about whether the report of it was accurate.

questions.explanation: A period of 24 hours and 12 minutes means the clock completes a cycle 12 minutes later than a 24-hour day would, so it gains 12 minutes against the sun every day, and it gains them in the same direction each time round. The consequences worth computing are the ones that make the point. Over 30 days the clock is 30 times 12 minutes ahead, which is 360 minutes, or 6 hours, and 6 hours is roughly the size of the difference between morning and evening in a person's own temperature rhythm, which is why a free-running person experiences a shifting mismatch. Over a year the gain is 365 times 12 minutes, which is 4,380 minutes, or 73 hours, or 3 days and one hour. So the clock has to be reset by something external about once a day, and a small daily correction of 12 minutes is enough; that is exactly what light does. The estimate itself should be quoted with its limits, since the studies involve very few people held under artificial conditions, and the period is an average across individuals whose own values differ.

questions.stem: A traveller crosses six time zones from west to east and another crosses six from east to west. Both are awake and alert for several days. What is the difference in what has happened to their clocks?

options.text: The eastward traveller's clock has stopped, since a shift of six zones exceeds what a clock can absorb
options.misconception: treats a six-zone shift as beyond the clock's capacity to adjust

questions.learningObjective: state what rebound sleep consists of after total deprivation

questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: Whether Sleep Consolidates What Was Learned
questions.learningObjective: state the evidence and the dispute about sleep and memory consolidation

options.misconception: dismisses the whole finding as a baseline effect

options.text: As a well-supported association with a live dispute about the mechanism, since protection from interference and active processing are hard to separate

options.misconception: asserts one side of a live dispute as the settled conclusion

Learning followed by sleep beats learning followed by waking, the effect is larger for material that had been studied in the evening, and the deep early-night sleep is the part that carries it, with the dreaming stage contributing more to the later part of the night. What that leaves open is the mechanism, and there are two live candidates. options.misconception: multiplies by the follow-up instead of dividing by the person-time

Tolerance is the first and the most familiar, and it is a change in the response rather than in the body's baseline: the same dose produces less effect, the dose needed for the same effect rises, and this is why the same quantity of a drug can be harmless once and dangerous later. Dependence comes next, and it is a change in the baseline: the body compensates for the drug's presence, so the ordinary state now sits below what the person feels when the drug is there, and it takes the drug to feel ordinary. Withdrawal is the consequence that follows from that, and it is what happens when the drug stops: the compensating changes are now unopposed, and the effects run in the opposite direction to the drug's, which is why a stimulant's withdrawal looks like a collapse in energy and a depressant's withdrawal looks like agitation. That is why the class is defined by its perceptual signature rather than by the property that groups the other two, and why the classification in use distinguishes substances by which of the three dimensions they move most. Two features of the class are worth knowing alongside the definition. The kinds of experience reported include altered forms and patterns without a person believing they are real, and a range of feelings from elation to acute fear, which is one reason some substances in the class have a long history of ceremonial use and also a substantial record of people having frightening experiences. questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: Why Altered States Are Hard to Study
questions.learningObjective: explain the methodological difficulty of studying a change in reported experience
questions.stem: Several claims about altered states rest only on what the people in them said afterwards. What is the central methodological problem with that?

options.text: The experiences are too rare to study, since altered states occur in only a small share of people
options.misconception: attributes the difficulty to how often the experiences occur

options.text: Nothing can be investigated, since a state by definition is private and therefore outside any science
options.misconception: generalises from privacy to the impossibility of investigation

options.text: The only available measure is a report, which is produced by a person who is also the one whose state is in question, and there is no outside criterion
Reports cannot be recorded accurately, since the people who make them are not trained to describe them
options.misconception: makes the problem an absence of training in describing rather than the absence of an outside check

questions.explanation: The problem is structural and it has a name in the methodology of this area: a demand characteristic in its strongest form, which is that the person who produces the report is the same person whose state is under examination, and the report is the only available measure. There is no outside criterion that would show the report to be wrong, since a person's account of an experience is the definition of the data, and the account is shaped by what they have been told, what they expect to have happened and what language they have for it. Three kinds of remedy exist and none of them eliminates the problem. Behaviour can be measured independently, and it usually disagrees with the report in instructive ways, as it does with accounts of pain and of the presence of other people. Outcomes with an independent criterion, such as performance on a task, can be studied even when the experience cannot be characterised. And comparison with a condition in which the person is told what to expect does a great deal, by making the two sources of the report diverge and showing where the expectation is doing the work. None of those is a clean solution, which is why claims of this kind are usually stated more carefully than the headline version suggests.
questions.hint: Ask who is producing the only available measure, and what that person is also the source of.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: A Claim That Rests on a Description Alone
questions.learningObjective: explain what a first-person report can and cannot establish
questions.stem: A researcher reports that during a state induced by fasting and a long walk, participants felt that their sense of self had dissolved and that time had slowed. Explain what this finding establishes and what it does not.

answer.exemplar: The finding establishes something real and worth taking seriously, and the discipline in question is being precise about the size of it. What it establishes is that people in that condition describe the experience in those terms, and that the reports have enough in common across participants to be worth analysing: the language recurs, the descriptions cluster around a reduced sense of a bounded self and a changed relation to time, and the accounts can be compared across people rather than treated as private curiosities. That is a genuine finding about reported experience, and describing one's own state is a legitimate kind of evidence about one's own state. What it does not establish is anything about the state itself, and the two gaps are specific. The first is the report as a measure. The person making it is the person being measured, the report is produced by a system that is part of what is being described, and the language available shapes what can be said, so the finding cannot distinguish between a change in experience, a change in the ability to describe experience, and a change in what the person expects to report. The second is the other direction. Even if the report were a perfect measure, a finding that the experience is describable in a particular way says nothing about what produced it, so a description of the state is compatible with several accounts of its cause and a description of its neural basis, and the finding discriminates between none of them. The way forward is not to discard reports, which are the only access there is to the experience itself, but to attach something independent to them: behaviour that can be observed, outcomes with an external criterion, or a comparison condition in which participants are told what to expect, so that the divergence between the two sources shows how much the expectation is contributing. A study that pairs the report with such a measure can say considerably more than one that has only the report, and a study that has only the report should state its claim as one about what people said.

questions.explanation: A good answer separates the two gaps. The report is evidence that people describe the state in those terms, and the recurrence of the language across participants is what makes it a finding rather than an anecdote. It is not evidence about the state itself, since the reporter and the reported are the same system and the language shapes what can be said, and it is not evidence about the cause, since a description is compatible with several accounts. It should propose pairing the report with an independent measure rather than discarding it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the reporter and the reported are the same system, and then ask what the description says about its own cause.

options.text: The participant is told that the session is over, and the suggestions operate only because the person believes the session has finished
options.misconception: reduces the effect to a belief about the session's status

options.text: A set of instructions is read while the participant is told to focus on a suggestion, and the participant reports or shows the suggested effect

options.misconception: requires the participant to be rendered unconscious by a substance

A participant is seated or lying in a quiet room, a script of instructions is read to them, and the script directs their attention to a particular sensation, often a heaviness of the arm or a fixed gaze, while telling them what to expect and inviting them to reserve a capacity for suggestions. What follows is that the participant is given a suggestion and something is measured: a report of an experience, an inability to move a limb, a change in pain or a performance on a task. And nothing is administered that is not on the list of things said, which is what makes the procedure studied as a social and psychological event. options.misconception: excludes the participants whose scores are low rather than analysing them separately

options.text: That the scores measure something other than suggestibility, since a reliable scale would not separate people so sharply
options.misconception: treats a bimodal distribution as evidence that the scale is measuring the wrong thing

options.text: That the variation is small, since the scores differ by less than the margin of error on the scale
options.misconception: invents a margin of error that makes the observed differences negligible

options.text: That an average over all participants blurs a real difference, so groups are formed on the score and effects are reported within them

Excluding the low scorers is not a neutral simplification, since it changes the population the conclusion is about and leaves the most common case unstudied. questions.hint: Ask what a mean across a widely spread group describes, and how a study should use the score.

10 percent deeply responsive and 32 percent moderately responsive, with the rest excluded as unclassified

options.text: 1 percent deeply responsive and 42 percent at least moderately responsive, since 100 out of 1,000 is one in a hundred

questions.learningObjective: state the two rival accounts of hypnosis and the evidence bearing on them
questions.stem: One account says hypnosis puts a person into a distinctive altered state, and another says it is a set of expectations and a willingness to follow instructions. How does the evidence bear on the dispute?

options.misconception: treats a report as decisive evidence for the state the report describes

options.misconception: declares both accounts unfalsifiable without trying to state a test

questions.learningObjective: explain the ethical problem with a post-hypnotic suggestion

options.text: The difficulty is only that the action may be foolish, since a person could be made to do anything at all
options.misconception: locates the problem in the wisdom of the action rather than in the absence of consent

options.text: The difficulty disappears if the person is asked afterwards whether they would have done it knowingly
options.misconception: treats a retrospective question as a way of obtaining valid prior consent

options.text: The person exercised no meaningful control at the time, so consent cannot be informed unless the mechanism and the signal are disclosed beforehand
There is no difficulty, since the person carried out the action and thereby consented to it by performing it
options.misconception: treats performance of an action as retrospective consent to being manipulated

questions.explanation: The difficulty is about consent rather than about the effect. Consent has two requirements that a post-hypnotic instruction removes at the same time: the person has to know what they are agreeing to, and they have to be free to refuse it. Neither holds at the moment of the action, since the person does not know that an instruction exists, does not know the signal is connected to it, and cannot decline a request they do not know has been made. That is why the standard is disclosure beforehand: the mechanism, the signal and the action have to be described during the consent process, so that the person can decide with the whole picture, and the great majority of research on the effect deliberately withholds the signal from the participant in order to study it at all. Nothing about the finding is prohibited, and the effect is well documented, but a study that uses it is doing something to a person that the person could not have agreed to if asked at the time. The second option mistakes the performance of an action for agreement, and the fourth is a retrospective question dressed up as consent.
questions.hint: Ask what the person would have had to know in order to refuse, and whether that knowledge was available.

options.misconception: applies a general arousal optimum to a task-specific and discontinuous decline

options.text: A motivation effect, in which the performer has not tried hard enough because the outcome matters less to them
options.misconception: explains a decline in performance as a decline in effort

options.text: A learning effect, in which the performance has been practised so often that it has become automatic and needs no attention
options.misconception: explains a decline by the automatisation of a practised skill

That discontinuity is what separates it from the general arousal relationship, which predicts a smooth optimum across a range of difficulties rather than a sudden collapse of something that had been reliable. The account usually given is that attention is reallocated. The steps of a well-learned skill have become automatic, and under pressure attention moves to the outcome, the audience, the consequence of failing and the score, which takes capacity away from the control of the skill itself; a task that was handled without attention now has none to spare. questions.explanation: The findings are substantial and the account of them is not settled. That a person can feel a limb that has been removed is common, and that the feeling can be vivid, can include movement and can be shaped by the person's intention towards the limb is also common. The brain imaging work is consistent with a persistent representation of the missing part rather than with its disappearance, and it shows that the map of the body reorganises after the loss, with the region that had represented the missing part showing responses when the person thinks about or intends to move it, and a neighbouring region's role increasing. What is debated is how the representation is maintained and how the sensations arise, and there is a second controversy about how a practitioner should treat them, since some procedures use the sensations to help a person regain use of the limb and their evidence base has been questioned. The second option offers a peripheral explanation that is both unnecessary and unable to account for sensations of a part that is not there at all. The remaining two are errors of logic: a sensation is a report, not an observation of what is present, and nothing about the phenomenon depends on how quickly the limb was lost.
questions.hint: Ask what the brain imaging shows about the region that represented the missing part, and what that tells you.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: Feeling Detached From the Body or the World
questions.learningObjective: state what a feeling of unreality describes and how common it is
questions.stem: A person says their own hands look unreal, that they are watching themselves from outside, or that the room around them seems like a stage set. What is the phenomenon, and what is its standing?

options.text: Schizophrenia, since feeling detached from one's own body is one of its defining symptoms
options.misconception: moves a common experience into a diagnosis on the strength of one symptom

options.text: A sleep-related phenomenon, since the feeling of unreality is characteristic of the moment of falling asleep
options.misconception: reduces the phenomenon to the moment of sleep onset

options.text: A sign of an injury to the temporoparietal region, since that region is known to produce the experience
options.misconception: treats a reported association with a region as a demonstrated lesion cause

options.text: Depersonalisation or derealisation, which are common experiences and only a disorder when they are distressing, persistent and disruptive

questions.explanation: The description is of depersonalisation, where the sense of ownership of one's own body or thoughts is altered, or derealisation, where the surroundings seem unreal. The first thing to know is that these are common: brief experiences of feeling detached or unreal occur in a substantial share of people, in situations of stress, fatigue, pain, grief, long journeys and unfamiliar surroundings, and they are also described in the transition into and out of sleep, which is where the third option comes from and why it is wrong to confine the phenomenon to that moment. What turns the experience into a disorder is not the experience but its consequences: it is persistent, it is distressing, and it interferes with ordinary life, and it is then commonly grouped with the dissociative conditions. A feeling of unreality that comes and goes with tiredness is not a disorder and does not need treatment. The second option takes one symptom and reads it as a diagnosis, which is a mistake worth naming, since the two conditions have different features, different courses and different treatments. The fourth turns an association into a demonstrated lesion, which is a stronger claim than the evidence supports.
questions.hint: Ask how often the experience occurs in people who are well, and what turns an experience into a disorder.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Sleep and Altered States: What Can Be Reported and What Can Be Explained
questions.learningObjective: synthesise the gap between describing a state and accounting for it
questions.stem: People can report in detail what an altered state is like, can say which experiences are stable across people, and can show that some of them are altered by a change in the brain. Synthesise what this combination of results establishes and what it leaves unexplained.

answer.exemplar: The three results are of different kinds, and the interesting part of the synthesis is that they do not add up to an account of anything. The first is phenomenological: the reports are detailed, they are internally coherent, they recur across people, and particular features are stable enough that a report can be recognised. That is a real result and it means a substantial amount can be said about what a state is like. The second is structural: the same experiences are found across a considerable range of people, which is what licenses treating a report as a description of a state rather than of one person's peculiarity, and it is what makes a taxonomy of states possible at all. The third is the one that usually gets overread. Changes to the brain alter the reports, and correlating a report with a pattern of activity is not the same as explaining why a particular pattern should give rise to that particular experience, because the same activity accompanies different experiences and the same experience arises from different patterns, and the correlations are drawn from a small literature with the usual problems of the field. Put the three together and the result is a system that is thoroughly characterised at the level of report, partially mapped at the level of the brain, and unaccounted for in the passage from one to the other. That gap is often described as the difficulty of explaining why any physical process should be accompanied by an experience, and it is a real gap in the explanation rather than an artefact of sloppy work, since the discipline has not been able to close it in any of the areas where it has been looked for. Two temptations should be named and resisted. The first is to treat the correlation with brain activity as the explanation, which converts a mapping into a mechanism and leaves the question of why that mechanism has the content it has entirely untouched. The second is to treat the gap as a licence for anything at all, on the reasoning that since nothing explains it, anything is as good; the constraints are real, and the states people report have properties that any account would have to accommodate. What the combination does establish is that the question is well posed, that it is answerable in principle, that a good deal of the input has been collected, and that what is missing is an account of the link rather than more data about either end.

questions.explanation: A good answer sorts the three results by what kind of claim they support: detailed and stable reports license describing a state, similar reports across people license treating a report as a description of a state, and a correlation with brain activity maps a state without explaining it. It should name the gap as the link between a physical process and the experience that accompanies it, and resist both reading a correlation as a mechanism and treating the gap as licence for any account at all.
questions.hint: Ask which of the three results is about report, which is about generality and which is about the brain, and what each can carry.
